actions.justification: Mandatory first step: assess current vital signs to establish baseline and identify hemodynamic instability or hypoxia in this patient with fever, cough, and dyspnea.
Mandatory: evaluate respiratory status including work of breathing, oxygen requirement, and breath sounds to characterize severity of pneumonia/respiratory illness.
Mandatory: chest X-ray is essential to confirm pneumonia, assess infiltrate distribution, and rule out pleural effusion or alternative diagnosis.
MANDATORY action — CBC is required as first step in CAP assessment to evaluate WBC count, assess severity, and guide management.
CURB-65 score is essential to stratify CAP severity and guide disposition (outpatient vs inpatient vs ICU). Should be done early in assessment phase.

BMP provides BUN for CURB-65 scoring, and electrolytes are critical to monitor given patient's long QT comorbidity — electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia) can worsen QT prolongation.

Patient presents with cough, fever, and dyspnea consistent with community-acquired pneumonia. After initial CURB-65 assessment, evaluate ICU admission criteria (severe CAP criteria) to guide level of care and treatment intensity.
Blood cultures should be obtained prior to initiating antibiotics per IDSA CAP guidelines to identify causative organism and guide targeted therapy.
Procalcitonin helps differentiate bacterial from viral pneumonia, supports antibiotic stewardship decisions, and can guide duration of therapy in CAP.

Patient presents with cough, fever, and dyspnea consistent with community-acquired pneumonia. Legionella urinary antigen test is recommended as part of standard CAP workup, especially to guide antibiotic selection and identify atypical pathogens.
Sputum culture should be obtained prior to antibiotic administration to identify causative organism and guide targeted therapy in CAP workup.

Patient with CAP (cough, fever, dyspnea) — beta-lactam plus macrolide is the standard first-line regimen per IDSA/ATS CAP guidelines. Note: patient has long QT syndrome, so a respiratory fluoroquinolone is contraindicated due to QT prolongation risk; beta-lactam plus macrolide combination is the safer choice.
Patient has CAP with fever and respiratory symptoms; IV fluids support hydration and hemodynamic stability while awaiting culture results and imaging. Already on beta-lactam plus macrolide therapy.

CAUTION: Patient has long QT syndrome, which is a relative contraindication to fluoroquinolones due to QT prolongation risk. However, given the available options and ongoing assessment, this should only be considered if coverage is inadequate and risk-benefit favors use with cardiac monitoring. Recommend deferring unless clinical deterioration warrants broader coverage.

Patient has long_QT comorbidity and has received both a respiratory fluoroquinolone and beta-lactam+macrolide — both classes prolong QT interval. Baseline/monitoring ECG is mandatory to assess QTc and risk of fatal arrhythmia.
Pneumococcal urinary antigen test is a guideline-recommended diagnostic for CAP (alongside Legionella antigen already ordered) to identify Streptococcus pneumoniae and guide antibiotic de-escalation.
Patient requires serial reassessment of respiratory and clinical status at 80 minutes post-arrival to evaluate response to antibiotics and fluid resuscitation, per CAP management guidelines.

Patient has known long QT syndrome and has received QT-prolonging agents (fluoroquinolone and macrolide). ECG was ordered; active monitoring of QT interval is mandatory to detect potentially life-threatening arrhythmias.
Serial assessment of SpO2 and oxygenation is indicated to detect clinical deterioration early and determine if escalation of care (supplemental oxygen, ICU transfer) is needed per CAP guidelines.

CBC, procalcitonin, blood cultures, sputum culture, and urine antigen tests are all pending. Reviewing results as they return guides antibiotic de-escalation or escalation decisions per CAP guidelines.
